metadata.title: How to Use SQLite in a Capacitor App (2026 Guide)
metadata.description: Learn how to use SQLite in a Capacitor app: pick a plugin, open a database, run migrations, transactions, encryption and web support, with working code.
metadata.author: Martin Donadieu

faq.question: What is the best SQLite plugin for Capacitor 8?
faq.answer: For new apps, @capgo/capacitor-fast-sql is a strong default: it supports iOS, Android and web (SQLite Wasm with OPFS), optional SQLCipher encryption, transactions, batches and BLOBs, and it moves query data over a local HTTP channel instead of the Capacitor bridge. @capacitor-community/sqlite is the mature alternative and is required if you want TypeORM's built-in capacitor driver.

faq.question: Can I use SQLite in a Capacitor app on the web?
faq.answer: Yes. Fast SQL uses the official @sqlite.org/sqlite-wasm build with OPFS persistence on the web. Your server must send Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin and Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp, otherwise the plugin falls back to a non-persistent database.

faq.question: How do I run schema migrations with SQLite in Capacitor?
faq.answer: Store the schema version in PRAGMA user_version, keep an ordered list of migration steps in your code, and on startup run every step newer than the stored version inside a transaction, bumping user_version at the end of each step. Never edit a step that already shipped.

faq.question: Is SQLite better than Capacitor Preferences or localStorage?
faq.answer: For more than a handful of values, yes. Preferences is meant for small key-value settings, and WebView storage like localStorage or IndexedDB can be evicted by the OS. SQLite gives you a real file on disk, indexes, transactions and queries.

faq.question: Does the database survive a Capgo live update?
faq.answer: Yes. Live updates replace the web bundle, not the app data directory, so the SQLite file stays. Your migration code ships with the bundle, so keep migrations additive so an older bundle can still read a newer schema after a rollback.

blocks.text: To use SQLite in a Capacitor app, install a native SQLite plugin such as

, open a database once at startup, create your schema with versioned migrations, then read and write with parameterized SQL. This guide walks through that full setup on Capacitor 8 for iOS, Android and the web, including transactions, encryption, file locations, and the errors you are most likely to hit.
If you only need a few settings, SQLite is overkill. If you store lists, records, or anything you want to filter, sort, or sync, it is the right tool.
When SQLite is the right storage choice
Capacitor apps have several places to put data. They solve different problems:
Lives inside the WebView, the OS can evict it, no real queries in localStorage
String values only, not meant for large data, not encrypted
Records, offline data, sync queues, search

Pick SQLite when you need any of these: offline-first data, more than a few hundred records, filters and sorting, relations between tables, atomic multi-step writes, or encryption at rest for structured data.

OPFS needs cross-origin isolation, so your dev server and your production host must send two headers:
If the headers are missing, the plugin logs a warning and falls back to a non-persistent database: everything works until you reload.

Two practical consequences. First, uninstalling the app deletes the file on both mobile platforms. Second, backups can restore the database file onto a new device. That is usually what you want, but if the database is encrypted with a key that does not travel with the backup, the restored file cannot be opened. The encryption guide covers how to handle that.
